doc.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Gary McFarland and Brotherhood of Man
summary: McFarland's fatal drink, and recording Brotherhood of Man three times in the same key.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Gary McFarland was a very, very suave, debonair, young, talented cat who – I know he loved Ellington, because we used to talk about it all the time. He was just a nice cat. He was a rather dangerous living cat. He’d – was wasting himself playing Russian roulette with a drink. He takes the – a person like him or Joe Maini. Joe Maini did it with a gun. Spin it around and walked to a cat’s house. Bam. Blew his brains all over the house. This cat did it with a drink. Three card Monty – switch switch switch switch – pick up – [Terry makes a swallowing sound] – wrong one.

I don’t know. It was some kind of poison in one of the drinks. I don’t know what it was. But the two drinks were good, and one was destined to take you on away from here. He got a hold of that one, and he went. But he was marvelous cat, marvelous player, good little vibe player, great writer. He had a lot of young, different ideas about . . .
What about the Brotherhood of Man piece?
Yeah, that’s one of the – I recorded that two – three times, I think. With him, with his big band. We did it with Mulligan, I think. And we did it with Oscar Peterson.
Did you find his treatment to be especially efficacious for you? or . . .
Ironically, all three of those records I made on that were pretty much the same, and I’m trying to remember which one I did first. I think it might have been Gerry . . .

McFarland, yeah. All three of them were in the same key, and I’m sure that the other two dates that we did after that date, they did it because it was in that key and the same tempo and everything. It had proven to be a fairly decent vehicle for me, so I guess they thought they’d stay in the same vein.
